en: Found the right words when taken unawares,
Found a guiding eye in darkness.
A surpassing lion, truly exceptional,
He was a true holy seer, a generous hero.
In darkness, if set upon a corsac fox's
Trail, he would not go astray.
When he spoke, all heard him.
From Manas, who had passed away,
This old man remained as a gift.
He girded his waist firmly.
If you ask of your uncle,
He was born in a holy place.
Your valiant uncle Bakay—
Those who saw his majesty were awed.
When he was a five-year-old child,
He studied in Mecca for five years.
He received a holy seer's blessing,
And was called Bakay the Saint.
He was a man of knowledge.
Even dead, his words would remain clear;
While alive, he was clairvoyant.
That was Bakay the lion.
Showing the land and waters,
Manas's orphan son
He led along this way.
A ridge like the curve of a saddle
Bakay came across.
When he came up onto the ridge,
If you ask of valiant Bakay,
He now turned Kokcholok's head,
And stood weeping profusely:
"Ah, my dear orphan,
My mind is bewildered.
This world, the merchant,
Seems to have cheated us and gone.
When Manas, the mountain-like lion, died,
When my hapless soul saw hell,
When Argyn and Kyrgyz together
Fled and migrated from Talas,
When fierce-maned Manas, the leopard—
The fire he had kindled went out,
When Manas Khan's caravan was left on foot,
When Abyke and Kobosh became masters of Talas,
Abyke and Kobosh—
Saying, 'God has utterly struck them down,'
The widows and the orphans
Were being plundered, they said,
I hear the tale from those who come,
I hear that this is the exact account.
Aruuke, daughter of Agynay,
Burulcha, daughter of Esen Khan,
The wife of my precious Alake—
If I continue from the learned accounts,
If I ask those who know,
This is what is known of them in captivity:
They seized them as spoils,
And did as they pleased, they say.
The widows and the orphans
They seized as spoils and prospered, they say.
When Akkula was shot down,
When Almambet died a martyr,
When my Almam went far away,
His horse's bridle was fastened.
In Aruuke's womb
Was a three-month child; she had pregnancy cravings.
'If my wife bears a boy,' he said—
That was my poor Almam's wish.
When toward Beijing, beyond even the Four Caliphs' reach,
They had drawn near,
Your precious Manas Khan was there,
All forty champions were there,
The deftest of the spearmen,
Mighty men who could shatter the world.
In China, Kaldai Khan was there,
All the heroes blessed by Kydyr were there.
Then, with his golden forelock and tasselled sash,
Aziz Khan's only son,
Cheerful Almambet was there as well.
Then Almambet stood
And spoke of his sorrow.
The sorrow he spoke of
Had a quality no one could forget.
He entrusted it to Bakay,
And gave him this charge:
'Holy seer who has seen many lands,
My fierce-maned elder uncle!
If you see Talas safe and sound,
If your affairs go well each day,
My wife Aruuke, Agynay's daughter—
If my wife gives birth safely,
Slaughter ninety for the feast.
If she bears a son,
Name him the hero Kulchoro!
If it is a boy,
His mount will be gray,
His fortune will be complete.
He will be a hero a spear's length beyond me.
He will be a blazing red ember,
The enemy he charges will be stopped.
Uncle Bakay, leopard,
It would be a disgrace not to heed me.
This is my trust in you.'
Those were Alake's words,
That was exactly what he said.
When she heard of Almambet,
She came before me,
Tearing her face and shrieking,
Sobbing, 'My valiant one!'
Her thoughts were shattered.
For six years, sinking down,
Her child had sunk within her.
For six years he remained undeveloped,
Then her child grew.
Aruuke gave birth, they say,
And banished all her grief, they say.
They slaughtered a mare for the feast,
And named him brave Kulchoro.
Unable to cherish her child fully,
Poor Aruuke
Saw the face of Judgment Day, they say.
She died three days later, they say.
An amulet was tied around his neck, they say.
'The heir left by my khan,' she said—
Poor Burulcha brought him up, they say.
When the child reached three,
Kobosh stirred up trouble, they say.
Coveting her beauty,
When the day cooled and evening fell,
They made her dance for entertainment.
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels
Took their revenge this way, they say.
The cattleherd in the gorge—
To that cattleherd, Bukosh
Was assigned as a milkmaid, they say.
By this time Burulcha's
Dress was worn and torn apart.
When Buko bent down,
Her buttocks showed behind.
Unable to cover her private flesh,
She had grown thin, I hear.
Called dead, she was not in a grave;
Called living, she was not counted among them.
Esen Khan's Burulcha
Was destitute, I hear.
The torments of Judgment Day
She was made to see, I hear.
If we do not go this very year,
She will die, I hear.
I heard the tale from those who came:
Almambet's Kulchoro—
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels,
To make him a slave for life,
Sent him after the sheep, they say.
Kulchoro would not submit to sheep-herding,
And humiliated the shepherd, they say.
He beat their horseherd,
And split open their pregnant mare.
A beauty such as Burulcha
The fool Abyke took, they say.
Your Alake's wife Burulcha
Would not let him enjoy her,
Would not let him lie in her embrace,
Would not yield herself, they say.
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels
Dragged her about and beat her, they say,
Left her mottled with blood, they say.
By the sheer cliff that echoes,
At the edge of the lone path,
Laying distress upon his neck,
She would not lie or rise in his embrace.
God struck those dogs down, they say;
They made her a neglected wife, they say.
They gave her a torn black yurt,
Gave her a black cow with a torn nostril,
Made her rise early in the morning,
Made her work rawhide.
For widows and the poor,
For orphans and the destitute,
For the blind and the lame,
He slaughtered their livestock in droves,
Gave feasts and brought them joy,
And depleted their herds, I heard.
Abyke, Kobosh, the six scoundrels:
'He sets fire to grassy lands,
The offspring of one cursed to burn!
He pours blood into clear water,
He has only reached six;
If he reaches fifteen, he will let no good come of it,
He will leave none of us unharmed!'
So saying this,
They took the whip to him and dragged him about.
Almambet's Kulchoro
They left mottled with blood, they say.
They tortured him, thrashed and beat him, they say.
Crying, 'Alas, father, why did you die?'
Kulchoro wept and sobbed.
Destitution had fallen upon his head;
Kulchoro cried out and wept.
His voice was heard by God;
He suffered terribly, I heard.
Barefoot and bareheaded,
Along the ridge at Urbust's summit,
He wanders about, I heard.
'When will my uncle come?' he asks,
Questioning everyone he sees,
Waiting anxiously, I heard.
If we do not go this very year,
My dear orphan,
If we do not rescue him,
Would he not know all our villainy?
On the coming Day of Judgment,
If what is told is true,
Would he not make us black donkeys and ride us?
His father, fierce-maned Almambet,
Was your father's sworn friend.
In Manas Khan's army
Were forty champion companions.
Each fierce-maned warrior, two by two,
Had a companion like a twin.
They threw the whole world into turmoil.
Every one was renowned;
They were all companions of equal standing.
Told to take a hat, they cut off a head;
Told to drink water, they drank poison;
Told to spill blood, they spilled the stomach's contents.
All those companions,
Let me enumerate them:
Azhybay and Bakay, twin khans,
Almambet and Chubak, twin heroes,
Syrgak and Serek, equals.
Hero Shuutu, with a hat like a yurt's felt roof,
The falcon of mankind,
Was himself the son of Angliya Khan.
Yraman's son, the Singer,
The lower khan's Tolgochu,
Tortkurongbek's darling.
Akzholtoy and matchless Tologu,
Serek, who drank Kaldai's blood,
Strong-armed Baychoro,
Akayar, who lifted camels,
Tazbaymat and Shuutu, those two were there.
At the head of the Forty was Kyrgylchal,
The crazy old man who grew arrogant among the Forty.
He devised a thousand mischiefs,
And left no quarrel untouched.
Your courser of a father, the leopard,
Would never say, 'He has ruined it.'
A creature of a treacherous soul,
Of fierce-maned Manas Khan,
He was not the one called Bozuul.
Though the Forty Companions turned aside,
Their precious lord was your Almam.
When he died a martyr in China,
When he died a martyr in Beijing,
They became wanderers—do you see?—
His wife and child.
